claims.text: Phase stability in high-temperature BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is primarily governed by a composition-dependent thermodynamic instability.
Adding Al lowers the free energy of competing ordered or intermetallic phases as temperature decreases.
The Al-induced lowering of competing-phase free energies reduces the thermodynamic stability of the BCC phase.
Sluggish atomic diffusion at intermediate temperatures delays transformation out of the BCC state.
The metastable BCC state persists until sufficient thermal activation is provided.
The initial Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 material can be processed into a high-temperature BCC structure by elevated-temperature solution processing.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion and predominantly retains the high-temperature metastable BCC phase.
The relevant intermediate-temperature transformation range is approximately 600–900 °C.
Local chemical ordering or clustering is driven by Al's affinity for ordered arrangements.
Local Al-associated ordering or clustering is a precursor to more stable ordered, intermetallic, or ordered-FCC phases.
Transformation from metastable BCC is controlled by competition between a thermodynamic driving force toward alternative phases and a kinetic barrier from sluggish diffusion.
Holding the alloy at intermediate temperature for sufficient time allows chemical ordering and transformation toward lower-free-energy phases.
Slow cooling or intermediate-temperature annealing will decrease the BCC phase fraction relative to rapid quenching.
Slow cooling or annealing will produce detectable ordered or intermetallic phases relative to the rapidly quenched control.
The proposed comparison keeps composition, atmosphere, and sample geometry constant while varying quenching, cooling rate, or intermediate-temperature annealing.
Failure to observe either a significant BCC-fraction reduction or emerging ordered/intermetallic phases after slow cooling or annealing would falsify the hypothesis.
